definitions.explanation: A person who is excessively kind and trusting, often to the point of being naive or easily taken advantage of. Can be used affectionately or critically.

examples.japanese: {彼|かれ}はお{人好|ひとよ}しだから{断|ことわ}れない。
そんなお{人好|ひとよ}しだと{騙|だま}されるよ。
examples.english: If you're that gullible, you'll get tricked.

examples.japanese: {母|はは}はお{人好|ひとよ}しで、{頼|たの}まれると{何|なん}でも{引|ひ}き{受|う}けてしまう。
examples.english: My mother is such a pushover that she takes on anything she's asked to do.

notes:
The nuance ranges from warm affection to gentle criticism depending on context. When used about someone you care about, it often carries a tone of "too kind for their own good." When used more critically, it implies the person is naive or a pushover. Composed of the honorific お + {人|ひと} (person) + {好|よ}し (good-natured).

USAGE:
Can function as a noun (「お{人好|ひとよ}しだ」) or as a modifier with の (「お{人好|ひとよ}しの{性格|せいかく}」). Often used with だから to explain why someone gets taken advantage of.

COMMON COLLOCATIONS:
- お{人好|ひとよ}しな{性格|せいかく}: a too-nice personality
- お{人好|ひとよ}しにも{程|ほど}がある: there's a limit to being too nice
- お{人好|ひとよ}しだと{損|そん}をする: being too nice will cost you

SIMILAR WORDS:
- {人|ひと}がいい: good-natured — a neutral description without the "too much" nuance
- お{人好|ひとよ}し is stronger, implying naivety
- {甘|あま}い: lenient; soft — describes someone who is too easy on others
- {世間知|せけんし}らず: naive about the world — more about lacking worldly experience
